headline: Ima ni is 今 (ima, “now”) plus に (ni).

sources.quote: 今(いま) (ima, “now”) + に (ni)

examples.ja: 今にわかる。
今に後悔するぞ。

headline: The old spelling of tabi, 単皮, means a single (単) hide (皮): originally a leather shoe.

sources.quote: /taɴbi/ → /tabi/
Shift in pronunciation from tanbi, the expected regular goon compound reading for the 単皮 spelling, which appears in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938 CE.

Originally referred to a leather shoe, which could be made from a single (単) animal hide (皮). As footwear in Japan developed, so too did the sense of tabi. The modern sense of a split-toed sock arose from at least the late Kamakura period, around the late 1200s, early 1300s. However, the leather shoe sense was still in use in 1603, as evidenced by the relevant entry in the Nippo Jisho.
The shift in reading was possibly influenced by the regular kun'yomi tabi of the term 旅 (tabi, “travel, voyage, trip”), as the tabi footwear was often worn for travel.

headline: Ku, “nine”, is from Early Middle Chinese 九, the goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Chinese 九 (MC kjuwX). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare vernacular Hokkien 九 (káu).

examples.ja: 彼は「九時だ」と言った。

headline: Hoteru is borrowed from English hotel, itself from French hôtel.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English hotel, from French hôtel.

examples.ja: ホテルは全焼した。
examples.en: The hotel was burned to the ground.

examples.ja: ホテルが見えてきた。

headline: Iidasu is ii, the stem of 言う (iu), plus 出す (dasu).

sources.quote: From 言(い)い (ii, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 言(い)う (iu)) + 出(だ)す (dasu).

examples.ja: これはだれかの言い出したことかい。
そんな事言い出すとは思わなかったよ。
examples.en: I didn't expect that to come from you.

meaning: to go back, to date back; ascend

sources.quote: Likely from Old Japanese, compound of 逆(さか) (saka, “reverse”) + 上(のぼ)る (noboru, “ascend, go up”).

examples.ja: 彼の家系は１７世紀にさかのぼる。

sources.quote: 天気 (tenki, “weather”) + 予報 (yohō, “forecast”)

headline: Risō may be a Japanese coinage from 理 (ri, “reason, principle”) plus 想 (sō, “thought, thinking”), first cited in an 1877 translation of Mill's Utilitarianism.

sources.quote: May be a coinage in Japanese from Chinese-based roots as a compound of 理(り) (ri, “reason, principle”) + 想(そう) (sō, “thought, thinking”).
First cited in Japanese to the 1877 translation of John Stuart Mill's Utilitarianism, 利学 (Rigaku) by 西周 (“Nishi Amane”).

examples.ja: 彼は私の理想の人よ。

sources.quote: Sinicization of 返(かえ)り事(ごと) (kaerigoto), from Old Japanese 返(かへ)り事(ごと) (kaferigoto, “reply, response”).

返事に困っている？

sources.quote: From 水(みず) (mizu, “water”) + 海(うみ) (umi, “sea”).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 植物 (MC dzyik mjut).

headline: Yōroppa is from Portuguese Europa; some sources say Dutch, but Dutch phonology makes that less likely.

sources.quote: /europpa/ [jeuɾoppa] → /joːroppa/
From Portuguese Europa.

Some references source this from Dutch Europa; however, Dutch phonology makes this less likely, as the ⟨eu⟩ vowel combination has apparently been pronounced as the monophthongs /œː/ or /øː/ since the time of Middle Dutch. Meanwhile, in Portuguese, the ⟨eu⟩ vowel combination has been pronounced as the diphthong /ew/, a closer match for the borrowed Japanese pronunciation.

Although this term is a 外来語 (gairaigo, “word of non-native or non-Middle Chinese origin”), it was borrowed early enough to be subject to the sound change from /eu/ to /joː/ during Late Middle Japanese. Compare similar developments in English (/ɛu̯/ → /juː/; /jʊ/, /jɔː/, /jɜː/ before /r/) during the Great Vowel Shift, which yields the modern English pronunciation of Europe.
Alternatively, it is merely a historical kana orthography-induced spelling pronunciation; compare 要(えう) (yō), as well as アルコール (arukōru).
Doublet of エウローペー (Eurōpē, “Europa”).

headline: Sorezore is a reduplication of それ (sore, “that”), with sore voiced to zore by rendaku.

sources.quote: Reduplication of それ (sore, “that”). The sore changes to zore as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Sei, “surname”, is from Middle Chinese 姓, the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 姓 (MC sjengH). The kan'on, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Min Nan reading sèⁿ.

examples.ja: 彼女は結婚前スミス姓だった。
examples.en: She was a Smith before her marriage.

examples.ja: あなたの姓が聞き取れなかった。
examples.en: I didn't get your last name.

headline: Sakai, “border”, is the stem of the obsolete verb 境う (sakau, “to divide, to form a boundary between things”).

sources.quote: /sakapi/ → /sakaɸi/ → /sakahi/ → /sakai/
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of obsolete verb 境う (sakau, “to divide, to form a boundary between things”).

Some sources further derive the verb as Old Japanese element 境 (saka, “division, border, boundary”) + auxiliary verb ふ (fu) indicating repetition or ongoing state. However, given the semantics, this could also be analyzed as the repetitive or ongoing aspect of Old Japanese-derived verb saku with an underlying meaning of “to split apart, to separate, to put distance between”, spelled variously as 割(さ)く, 裂(さ)く, 離(さ)く, or 放(さ)く, and cognate with 咲(さ)く (saku, “to bloom”, from the idea of the blooms splitting open), 栄(さか)える (sakaeru, “to prosper”, extended from the bloom sense), and 盛(さか)る (sakaru, “to be in prime condition, to prosper, to flourish”).

headline: Atatameru is the root of 暖か (atataka, “warm”) plus -meru, “-en, -ify”.

sources.quote: From あたた (atata, root of the adjective 暖(あたた)か (atataka, “warm”)) + める (-meru, “-en, -ify”)

examples.ja: 氷を温めるととける。
examples.en: If you heat ice, it melts.

headline: Daishō is 大 (dai, “big, large”) plus 小 (shō, “small, little”): size as “big-small”.

sources.quote: Compound of 大(だい) (dai, “big, large”) + 小(しょう) (shō, “small, little”).

examples.ja: 道路上の大小の石に気をつけなさい。
examples.en: Watch out for big and small stones on the road!

headline: Kanjō is probably a Middle Chinese compound, literally “investigate + to make something settled”.

sources.quote: Probably from Middle Chinese compound 勘定 (khom? dengᴴ, literally “investigate + to make something settled”). Compare modern Mandarin 勘定 (kāndìng, “to demarcate, to examine”).

examples.ja: 勘定は勘定。
お勘定です。

headline: The abacus reached Japan from China in the Muromachi period (1336–1573), and soroban is first attested in a 1595 trilingual dictionary.

sources.quote: Japanese sources consistently describe the abacus itself as being imported to Japan from China some time during the Muromachi period (1336–1573), although there is some disagreement as to whether this happened early in the period, or late.

First attested with the reading soroban in the 1595 trilingual Latin-Portuguese-Japanese dictionary Dictionarium Latino Lusitanicum, Ac Iaponicum, also 羅葡日対訳辞書 (Ra-Ho-Nichi Taiyaku Jisho, “Latin-Portuguese-Japanese Translation Dictionary”) based on work originally by Ambrogio Calepino, corroborated in the Nippo Jisho of 1603.

Japanese sources generally describe the soroban reading as a shift or corruption from the reading swanpan, the 唐音 (tōon, literally "Tang sound", referring to the Chinese-derived kanji readings that were borrowed into Japanese during the Tang dynasty or later) for the kanji spelling. However, this is problematic on phonological grounds:
* There is no known phonological process whereby swan would become soro in Japanese.
* Middle Chinese swan consistently became Japanese san in all other known instances of the Chinese reading swan for any kanji character.
* The character 算 appearing as the first character in 算盤 (soroban) is also read as san, and san is similarly listed as a synonym for soroban in the 1595 dictionary entry.

An alternative, albeit speculative, explanation is that this soro- is some other morpheme unrelated to the Chinese. If so, this might be native root soro-, as seen in adverb そろそろ (sorosoro, “quietly and calmly”), そろり (sorori) and そろっと (sorotto, “quietly and smoothly; slidingly, glidingly”), verb 揃う (sorou, “to be in alignment; to be in order; to match, to go together”).

Notably, this term appears historically with the alternative kanji spelling 三羅盤. Given the expected Japanese readings of these characters, this may have been read as saraban. Root sara- -- and also root suru- -- also appear in various terms related to senses of smooth, gliding, sliding.

headline: Yo was spelled with the phonetic 用 in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and has since taken on a more literary sense.

sources.quote: ⟨yo₁⟩ → /jʷo/ → /jo/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yo.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE with the phonetic spelling 用.
In modern development, this term has taken on a more literary sense.

headline: Sugi's kanji 杉 is an ateji (当て字), and the word is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 杉 (sugi₂), which Miyake (1997) (apud Schuessler, 2007) associates with Old Chinese 松 (OC *sɢloŋ). Ultimately comes from reconstructed Proto-Japonic *sunkOi.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
This kanji is an ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

examples.ja: 昔そこにはスギの大木があった。
examples.en: There used to be a large cedar tree there.

headline: Shima, “island”, is possibly related to Baekje 斯麻 (*syema, “island”) and Middle Korean 셤 (syem).

sources.quote: /sima/ → /ɕima/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *sima.
Possibly related to Baekje 斯麻 (*syema, “island”) and Middle Korean 셤 (syem), whence modern Korean 섬 (seom, “island”).

examples.ja: 島が見えてきた。
遠くに島が見えた。
examples.en: We saw an island in the distance.

meaning: to condemn, to blame, to criticize
headline: Semeru is from the classical lower bigrade verb せむ, cognate with 攻める (semeru) and 狭い (semai).

sources.quote: From the classical lower bigrade verb(マ行下二段活用) せむ. Cognate with 攻(せ)める (semeru), 迫(せま)る (semaru), 狭(せば)める (sebameru), 狭(せば)まる (sebamaru), and 狭(せま)い (semai).

examples.ja: 彼は私の過失を責めた。
examples.en: He accused me of my mistake.

examples.ja: 責められるべきは私だ。
examples.en: It is I that am to blame.
